questions.q: Identify the four main supporting characters in "Tomorrow" and state each one's primary relationship to Captain Hagberd.
questions.a: The four main supporting characters are: (1) Miss Bessie Carvil — Hagberd's tenant and sole confidante who listens to his ravings across the fence; (2) Josiah Carvil — Hagberd's blind, tyrannical tenant and Bessie's father, whose domestic oppression mirrors Hagberd's emotional tyranny; (3) Harry Hagberd — the captain's long-lost son whose actual return shatters the father's fantasy; (4) The Barber — the town wit who mocks Hagberd and believes chaffing can "cure" his madness. A wrong answer (e.g., listing the stranger at the gate as a main character, or omitting Harry) reveals the student cannot distinguish between fleeting plot devices and characters who structurally shape the protagonist's arc.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Bessie Carvil never contradicts Captain Hagberd's insistence that Harry will return "tomorrow," despite knowing it is a delusion.
questions.a: Bessie withholds contradiction because the one time she gently suggested Harry might be drowned, Hagberd reacted with "an expression of horror and incredulity, as though he had seen a crack open out in the firmament," terrifying her into silence. She realizes his madness has "its equilibrium based upon self-esteem" — disturbing it could unhinge him completely. She also feels "it was easier to half believe it myself" because her own life of drudgery under her father offers no alternative hope. A wrong answer (e.g., "she is kind" or "she loves him") reveals superficial reading: it misses the psychological complexity of her complicity — she sustains his delusion not just from pity but from her own desperate need for a future different from her present.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "character foil" to compare Old Carvil and Captain Hagberd. Identify two specific parallels and one crucial difference in how each exercises control over their dependent.
questions.a: Parallels: (1) Both are aging, isolated men who dominate a younger dependent — Carvil his daughter Bessie, Hagberd his imagined son Harry (and by extension Bessie). (2) Both use verbal aggression: Carvil "bellowed at the top of his voice... as if to defy Heaven," Hagberd launches into "flings and jerks and wicked side glances" when his narrative is doubted. Difference: Carvil's control is physical and immediate — he "would not lift his hand... would not move a limb... without calling her to his side and hanging all his atrocious weight on her shoulder" — while Hagberd's control is psychological and future-oriented: he prepares a house "for tomorrow," withholds the present, and traps Bessie in a deferred promise. A wrong answer that only lists similarities reveals inability to analyze how Conrad uses the foil to highlight Hagberd's particular madness — a madness of anticipation rather than present possession.

questions.q: Analyze how Harry Hagberd's physical appearance, speech, and actions in his first encounter with Bessie (pages 52-56) systematically dismantle his father's constructed fantasy of a "clever-looking, high-spirited boy" who will settle into domestic bliss.
questions.a: Harry arrives "tall," "powerful shoulder," "broad-brimmed shadow of a hat," radiating restless energy — not the boy of fourteen but a man of thirty-one shaped by sixteen years of wandering. His speech is cynical, colloquial ("the devil he is," "five quid," "dam'"), peppered with sailor's slang and capstan songs, revealing a life "boundary rider... sheared sheep... humped my swag... harpooned a whale." He mocks his father's "rabbit-hutches," calls the prepared home a "cage," and admits he came only for "five quid" from a "loving parent." His kiss of Bessie is "overmastering ardour... as if in haste to get at her very soul," then he demands money and leaves. Each detail contradicts the father's static, domestic fantasy: Harry is movement, not settlement; appetite, not patience; the world, not Colebrook. A wrong answer that merely lists Harry's jobs misses the analytical task: showing how Conrad choreographs the son's entrance as a systematic demolition of the father's delusion.

questions.q: Evaluate the Barber's claim that "every mental state, even madness, has its equilibrium based upon self-esteem. Its disturbance causes unhappiness." Does the story validate or undermine this theory? Support your judgment with two textual instances.
questions.a: The story *undermines* the Barber's theory. Instance 1: When the stranger (Harry) confronts Hagberd at the gate, Hagberd's equilibrium *shatters* — he paces wildly, gestures, shouts "I've had it for years — for years — for years — enough to last me till to-morrow," then flees indoors, bolting the door. His self-esteem cannot absorb the intrusion of reality. Instance 2: When Harry actually appears at the window, Hagberd denies his own son: "A grinning information fellow... Don't you have anything to do with him. It will spoil everything." The "equilibrium" is not self-esteem but a sealed delusion that *requires* the absence of the real Harry. The Barber's "cure by chaffing" fails because Hagberd's madness is not a superficial eccentricity but a survival structure built on the *permanent deferral* of "tomorrow." A wrong answer that agrees with the Barber reveals failure to see that Conrad portrays madness as a fortress, not a balance — and the Barber himself is part of the town's collective failure to understand.

questions.q: Create a 50-word diary entry from Bessie Carvil's perspective on the night Harry leaves, capturing her emotional shift from awakening to re-entrapment. Use one metaphor from the text.
questions.a:
"Tonight the wave broke over me — his kisses, his contempt, his leaving. I thought the tomorrow had come, but it was only another tonight. Father roars for tea. Captain Hagberd chuckles above: 'One day more.' I am the shore the sea abandons. No ship. No horizon. Only the tolling bell."
Criteria: Must show (a) the metaphor of the sea/wave from page 61 ("as if the sea... had sent a wave over her head"), (b) the collapse of hope ("tomorrow" vs "tonight"), (c) the return to dual imprisonment (father + Hagberd), (d) present-tense immediacy. A poor answer writes a generic sad diary entry without the text's specific imagery or Bessie's unique voice — revealing the student cannot inhabit a character's perspective using the author's own symbolic language.
